summary: Yellow flag iris is a wetland plant with showy yellow flowers that has invaded stream and pond edges, floodplains, shorelines and marshes. It spreads quickly through thick underground stems and forms dense stands that crowd out cattails and native irises. Its roots form a dense mat that compacts the soil, and large stands can reduce habitat for native fish and waterfowl and clog streams. All parts of the plant are toxic to livestock and other animals.
history: Yellow flag iris is native to Europe, Asia and northern Africa. It was brought to North America as an ornamental plant as early as the late 1700s, and has since been planted on purpose for gardens, erosion control and sewage treatment ponds. It is now found in all but four U.S. states.
seasons: Shoots come up in spring, and in mild winters they can stay green all year. It flowers from late May into early July, though plants usually don't flower until their third year. Seeds form from August through October and can float for more than a year, spreading along waterways.

handling.text: All parts of yellow flag iris are toxic to livestock and other animals.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
